questions.question: Should I brush my teeth before bed?
questions.answer: Yes, you should brush your teeth before bed every night.
questions.description: Brushing before bed removes the plaque and food debris that build up during the day. Saliva flow drops sharply during sleep, so bacteria left on your teeth have hours to produce enamel-eroding acids with little natural defense. Brush for two minutes with fluoride toothpaste, then spit rather than rinse so the fluoride stays on your teeth.
questions.reasoning: When you sleep, your mouth produces less saliva, which normally helps wash away food particles and neutralize acids. This creates an ideal environment for bacteria to thrive. Brushing before bed removes the bacterial film (plaque) and food debris that would otherwise feed harmful bacteria for 6-8 hours while you sleep.
questions.scientificBasis: The American Dental Association recommends brushing twice daily for two minutes with fluoride toothpaste. Studies show that nighttime brushing significantly reduces the risk of dental caries and periodontal disease.
questions.exceptions: If you've just had something acidic (citrus, soda, wine), some dentists suggest waiting 30-60 minutes before brushing so you don't scrub softened enamel.

questions.question: Should I wash my hands after using the restroom?
questions.answer: Yes, you should always wash your hands after using the restroom.
questions.description: Washing your hands after using the restroom is one of the most important hygiene practices for preventing the spread of germs and disease. Even if you don't directly touch contaminated surfaces, bacteria and viruses can be present in restroom environments and on surfaces like door handles, flush levers, and faucets.
questions.reasoning: Restrooms harbor numerous pathogens including E. coli, norovirus, salmonella, and other harmful bacteria and viruses. These microorganisms can cause gastrointestinal illnesses, respiratory infections, and other diseases. Proper handwashing with soap and water for at least 20 seconds removes these pathogens and prevents transmission to yourself and others.
questions.scientificBasis: The CDC identifies handwashing as one of the most effective ways to prevent the spread of infection. Community handwashing education has been shown to reduce diarrheal illness by roughly 23-40% and respiratory illnesses such as colds by about 16-21%.

questions.question: Should I wear sunscreen every day?
questions.answer: Yes, you should wear sunscreen every day, even when it's cloudy or you're indoors near windows.
questions.description: Daily sunscreen use protects your skin from harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation that can cause premature aging, sunburn, and skin cancer. UV rays penetrate through clouds and windows, meaning you're exposed even on overcast days or while indoors. Dermatologists recommend using broad-spectrum sunscreen with at least SPF 30 on all exposed skin.
questions.reasoning: UV radiation damages DNA in skin cells, leading to mutations that can cause skin cancer, and it drives most visible skin aging (photoaging). UVA rays penetrate clouds and window glass; UVB rays cause burning and are strongest at midday but present year-round. In a long-term randomized trial in Australia, regular sunscreen use roughly halved melanoma incidence and reduced squamous cell carcinoma by about 40%.
questions.scientificBasis: The American Academy of Dermatology states that daily sunscreen use is one of the most effective ways to prevent skin cancer and premature aging. Multiple long-term studies have demonstrated that regular sunscreen application significantly reduces skin cancer incidence.
questions.exceptions: Babies under 6 months should be kept out of direct sun with shade and clothing rather than relying on sunscreen.

questions.question: Should I drink eight glasses of water per day?
questions.answer: No, the 'eight glasses a day' rule is not scientifically supported. Your water needs depend on your size, activity level, climate, and overall health.
questions.description: While staying hydrated is important, the specific recommendation of eight 8-ounce glasses (about 2 liters) daily lacks scientific basis and doesn't account for individual variation. Most healthy people can rely on their thirst mechanism to determine when to drink. Water needs vary based on body size, physical activity, temperature, humidity, and health conditions. You also get water from food and other beverages.
questions.reasoning: The origin of the eight-glasses myth is unclear, but it may have come from a 1945 recommendation that was misinterpreted. That guidance suggested about 2.5 liters of water daily but included water from all sources, including food. Modern research shows that fluid needs vary dramatically between individuals. Athletes need more, as do people in hot climates. About 20% of daily fluid intake typically comes from food.
questions.scientificBasis: The National Academy of Medicine suggests adequate fluid intake is about 3.7 liters for men and 2.7 liters for women from all beverages and foods. However, they note that most healthy people can adequately meet their hydration needs by drinking when thirsty. No scientific evidence supports the specific eight-glasses recommendation.
questions.exceptions: People with kidney stones, endurance athletes, those working in heat, and people who are vomiting or have diarrhea may need deliberate extra fluids. Some heart and kidney conditions require fluid limits; follow your clinician's advice.

questions.question: Should I floss my teeth every day?
questions.answer: Yes, you should clean between your teeth once a day. Floss is one option; interdental brushes or water flossers work too.
questions.description: Flossing removes plaque and food debris from between teeth and under the gumline, areas that toothbrushes cannot effectively clean. This prevents cavities between teeth, reduces gum disease risk, and helps prevent bad breath. Flossing is especially important before bed to remove accumulated debris from the day.
questions.reasoning: About 40% of tooth surfaces are between teeth where toothbrush bristles cannot reach. Plaque that remains in these areas hardens into tartar, which can only be removed by a dental professional. This buildup leads to gingivitis (gum inflammation) and can progress to periodontitis (severe gum disease) that damages bone and can result in tooth loss. Flossing disrupts bacterial colonies before they can cause damage.
questions.scientificBasis: The American Dental Association recommends cleaning between teeth daily. A 2019 Cochrane review found low-certainty evidence that flossing plus brushing reduces gingivitis compared with brushing alone, and that interdental brushes may work better than floss where gaps allow. The evidence is limited mainly because long-term flossing trials are hard to run, not because flossing has been shown not to work.

questions.question: Should I take a multivitamin every day?
questions.answer: No, most healthy adults eating a balanced diet do not need a daily multivitamin. Getting nutrients from whole foods is preferable.
questions.description: For most healthy adults consuming a varied diet, multivitamins provide little to no health benefit. Research shows they don't reduce risk of heart disease, cancer, or cognitive decline in well-nourished populations. Some people may benefit from specific supplements (like vitamin D in winter, B12 for vegans, or folate for pregnant women), but blanket multivitamin use isn't supported by evidence.
questions.reasoning: Large-scale studies have consistently failed to show that multivitamins prevent chronic diseases or extend life in people without nutritional deficiencies. Nutrients from whole foods are better absorbed and come with beneficial fiber, antioxidants, and other compounds. Excessive supplementation can even be harmful—high doses of certain vitamins and minerals can cause toxicity or interfere with medications. Money spent on multivitamins is better invested in quality whole foods.
questions.scientificBasis: In 2022 the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force found insufficient evidence for multivitamins to prevent cancer or cardiovascular disease and recommended against beta-carotene and vitamin E supplements. The Physicians' Health Study II found no cardiovascular benefit, and a 2024 analysis of about 390,000 U.S. adults found daily multivitamin use was not associated with lower mortality.
questions.exceptions: Anyone who could become pregnant should take 400-800 mcg of folic acid daily. Vegans often need B12, and people with diagnosed deficiencies, bariatric surgery, or certain medical conditions may need specific supplements as advised by a clinician.

questions.question: Should I get a flu shot every year?
questions.answer: Yes, most people should get an annual flu vaccination to protect themselves and others from influenza.
questions.description: Annual flu vaccination is recommended for everyone six months and older, with rare exceptions. The flu vaccine protects against the most common circulating strains each season and significantly reduces your risk of severe illness, hospitalization, and death from influenza. It also helps protect vulnerable people around you who may be at higher risk of complications.
questions.reasoning: Influenza viruses change constantly, and vaccine protection wanes over months, so the vaccine is updated and given every season. Flu causes thousands to tens of thousands of U.S. deaths each year. When the vaccine is well matched to circulating strains, it reduces the risk of flu illness needing medical care by roughly 40-60%, and vaccinated people who still get sick tend to have less severe illness. Widespread vaccination also helps protect people who can't be vaccinated or respond poorly.
questions.scientificBasis: The CDC's Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices recommends annual flu vaccination for all persons aged six months and older. Clinical trials and observational studies consistently demonstrate vaccine effectiveness in reducing flu illness, medical visits, hospitalizations, and deaths.
questions.exceptions: Talk to a clinician first if you've had a severe allergic reaction to a previous flu vaccine or developed Guillain-Barre syndrome within six weeks of one. The nasal spray vaccine isn't suitable for everyone (for example, during pregnancy or with a weakened immune system).

questions.question: Should I wear a seatbelt every time I'm in a car?
questions.answer: Yes, you should always wear a seatbelt in a vehicle, regardless of where you're sitting or how short the trip.
questions.description: Seatbelts are the single most effective safety device in vehicles. For front-seat passenger car occupants they reduce the risk of fatal injury by 45% and moderate-to-critical injury by 50%. They spread crash forces across the strongest parts of your body and prevent ejection, which is almost always deadly.
questions.reasoning: In a collision, an unrestrained occupant keeps moving at the vehicle's pre-crash speed until hitting the interior, another person, or the road after ejection. Even at 30 mph, the impact is comparable to falling from a three-story building. Airbags are designed to work with seatbelts and can seriously injure unbelted occupants. Roughly half of the passenger vehicle occupants killed in U.S. crashes each year were not wearing seatbelts.
questions.scientificBasis: Decades of crash data show large reductions in deaths and injuries with seatbelt use. NHTSA estimates seatbelts save around 15,000 lives in the U.S. each year, and studies across many countries consistently show the same pattern.

questions.question: Should I exercise regularly?
questions.answer: Yes, you should engage in regular physical activity for both physical and mental health benefits.
questions.description: Regular exercise provides profound health benefits including reduced risk of heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes, several cancers, depression, and anxiety. It strengthens bones and muscles, improves cognitive function, enhances sleep quality, and increases longevity. Adults should aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity or 75 minutes of vigorous activity per week, plus muscle-strengthening activities twice weekly.
questions.reasoning: Physical inactivity is one of the leading risk factors for death worldwide. Exercise improves cardiovascular health by strengthening the heart, lowering blood pressure, and improving cholesterol profiles. It helps regulate blood sugar, maintain healthy body weight, and preserve muscle mass and bone density with aging. Exercise also releases endorphins and other neurochemicals that improve mood and reduce stress. The benefits are dose-dependent—more activity generally provides greater benefits, though even small amounts help.
questions.scientificBasis: Thousands of studies demonstrate exercise benefits across multiple health outcomes. The Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, based on comprehensive research review, recommend specific amounts and types of exercise for different populations. Meta-analyses consistently show strong associations between physical activity and reduced risk of chronic diseases and mortality.

questions.question: Should I sleep eight hours every night?
questions.answer: Roughly, yes. Most adults need at least 7 hours a night, and 7-9 hours suits most people; eight is a good target, not a magic number.
questions.description: Adequate sleep is essential for physical health, cognitive function, emotional regulation, and overall wellbeing. While individual needs vary slightly, most adults function best with 7-9 hours of sleep. Chronic sleep deprivation increases risk of obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, weakened immunity, depression, and cognitive decline. Quality sleep improves memory consolidation, problem-solving, creativity, and mood.
questions.reasoning: During sleep, your body performs critical maintenance including tissue repair, muscle growth, protein synthesis, and hormone regulation. The brain consolidates memories and clears metabolic waste. Insufficient sleep disrupts these processes and impairs judgment, reaction time, and emotional regulation. Sleep deprivation affects the hormones that regulate hunger, leading to increased appetite and weight gain. It also weakens immune function, making you more susceptible to infections.
questions.scientificBasis: A consensus statement from the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and Sleep Research Society recommends 7 or more hours per night for adults. Teenagers need 8-10 hours. Both short sleep and very long sleep are associated with health risks, though long sleep may often reflect underlying illness rather than cause it.

questions.question: Should I smoke cigarettes?
questions.answer: No, you should never smoke cigarettes. Smoking is the leading cause of preventable death and has no safe level of consumption.
questions.description: Cigarette smoking causes cancer, heart disease, stroke, lung diseases, diabetes, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). It harms nearly every organ in the body and increases risk of death from all causes. Smoking causes more than 480,000 deaths annually in the United States alone. Quitting smoking at any age provides immediate and long-term health benefits, and numerous effective resources exist to help people quit.
questions.reasoning: Tobacco smoke contains more than 7,000 chemicals, hundreds of them toxic and about 70 known to cause cancer. They damage DNA, impair immune function, cause inflammation, and narrow blood vessels. Nicotine is highly addictive, which makes quitting hard but very achievable with support. Even light or social smoking carries significant risk, and secondhand smoke causes disease and death in nonsmokers, particularly children.
questions.scientificBasis: Decades of research unequivocally demonstrate that smoking is catastrophically harmful to health. The U.S. Surgeon General's reports, based on thousands of studies, establish smoking as a direct cause of numerous diseases. No tobacco product is safe, and there is no risk-free level of exposure to tobacco smoke.

questions.question: Should I get an annual physical checkup?
questions.answer: Regular preventive care is worthwhile, but a full physical every single year isn't necessary for every healthy adult. How often you go should depend on your age, health, and the screenings you're due for.
questions.description: Regular checkups allow for early detection of health problems, monitoring of chronic conditions, updating vaccinations, and discussing preventive measures. While healthy younger adults may not need annual visits, most people benefit from periodic health assessments. Your doctor can perform screenings, review medications, assess risk factors, and provide personalized health guidance. The specific tests and frequency depend on age, sex, family history, and existing conditions.
questions.reasoning: Many serious conditions like high blood pressure, diabetes, and high cholesterol have no symptoms in early stages but can be detected through routine screening. Early detection generally leads to better treatment outcomes and can prevent complications. Regular visits also establish a relationship with your provider, making it easier to address concerns when they arise. Preventive care including vaccinations, cancer screenings, and lifestyle counseling can significantly reduce disease risk and improve quality of life.
questions.scientificBasis: A 2019 Cochrane review of general health checks in adults found they had little or no effect on overall mortality or cardiovascular deaths. Targeted preventive services do have strong evidence, and the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force publishes which screenings and vaccines are recommended at each age.
questions.exceptions: People with chronic conditions, those taking regular medications, older adults, and anyone with new symptoms should see a clinician as often as their care requires.

questions.question: Should I change my passwords regularly?
questions.answer: No, you don't need to change passwords regularly unless there's evidence of compromise. Focus on using strong, unique passwords instead.
questions.description: Contrary to old advice, mandatory periodic password changes often reduce security because people tend to make predictable modifications (like adding a number) or write passwords down. Modern security guidance emphasizes using strong, unique passwords for each account, enabling two-factor authentication, and changing passwords only when there's reason to believe they've been compromised. Password managers make it easy to maintain complex, unique passwords.
questions.reasoning: Frequent password changes encourage poor practices like simple patterns, password reuse, or writing passwords down. Research shows this actually decreases security. Strong, random passwords that are unique to each service are far more effective. When breaches occur, affected services notify users to change passwords. Using a password manager and two-factor authentication provides much better security than routine password rotation.
questions.scientificBasis: NIST's Digital Identity Guidelines (SP 800-63B, Revision 4, finalized in 2025) state that services must not require periodic password changes, but must force a change when there is evidence of compromise. The guidance favors long passwords, screening against lists of breached passwords, password managers, and phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication.

questions.question: Should I back up my computer data regularly?
questions.answer: Yes, you should regularly back up important data to protect against hardware failure, theft, ransomware, and accidental deletion.
questions.description: Regular backups are essential for protecting irreplaceable files like photos, documents, and work files. Hard drives and computers fail, devices get stolen or damaged, and ransomware can encrypt your files. The 3-2-1 backup rule recommends keeping three copies of data on two different types of media with one copy stored off-site. Cloud backup services and external hard drives make this easier than ever.
questions.reasoning: Every storage device eventually fails, often without warning. Without backups, a dead drive, a stolen laptop, a spilled drink, or a ransomware infection can mean permanent loss. Ransomware can also encrypt backups that stay connected to your computer, which is why at least one copy should be offline or off-site. Automated backups, tested occasionally by restoring a file, mean you can recover with minimal loss.
questions.scientificBasis: The 3-2-1 strategy (three copies, two different media, one off-site) is widely recommended by cybersecurity and disaster-recovery professionals, including CISA. Keeping at least one copy offline or immutable is a core ransomware defense.

questions.answer: No. Public WiFi is much safer than it used to be because most websites now encrypt traffic, but you should still take a few simple precautions.
questions.description: Today most websites and apps encrypt traffic with HTTPS, so someone on the same coffee-shop network usually can't read your passwords or messages. For sensitive tasks on an untrusted network, using your phone's cellular connection or a reputable VPN adds protection.
questions.scientificBasis: The FTC notes that most websites now use encryption, which protects information sent over public WiFi, while advising people to stay alert to unencrypted sites and fake networks. Security agencies continue to recommend keeping software updated and using encrypted connections for sensitive activity.

questions.question: Should I recycle plastic?
questions.answer: Yes, you should recycle plastic when possible, but reducing plastic consumption is even more important.
questions.description: Recycling plastic conserves resources, reduces landfill waste, and decreases pollution compared to producing new plastic. However, not all plastic is recyclable, and much plastic waste isn't actually recycled even when placed in recycling bins. Check your local recycling guidelines for which plastics are accepted. The most effective approach is reducing plastic use, reusing items when possible, and recycling as a last resort (the 'reduce, reuse, recycle' hierarchy).
questions.reasoning: Plastic production uses fossil fuels and creates greenhouse gas emissions. Recycling plastic uses less energy than creating virgin plastic, though the process isn't perfect—plastic can typically only be recycled a few times before quality degrades. Contamination and sorting challenges mean actual recycling rates are low (only about 9% of all plastic ever produced has been recycled). However, recycling is still better than disposal. The most impactful actions are refusing single-use plastics and choosing products with less packaging.
questions.scientificBasis: A 2017 global analysis estimated that only about 9% of all plastic waste ever produced has been recycled. The EPA and environmental organizations rank source reduction above recycling. Putting non-accepted items in the bin ('wishcycling') can contaminate whole loads, so follow your local program's rules.

questions.question: Should I eat breakfast every day?
questions.answer: No, eating breakfast isn't necessary for everyone. Listen to your body's hunger cues and eat when you're genuinely hungry.
questions.description: The idea that breakfast is the most important meal of the day isn't supported by strong scientific evidence. While some people feel and perform better eating breakfast, others naturally prefer to eat later in the day. What matters more is your overall diet quality and total daily nutrition, not the timing of your first meal. Some research suggests potential benefits from time-restricted eating (like skipping breakfast), though results are mixed.
questions.reasoning: The breakfast myth largely originated from marketing and observational studies that showed correlations (not causation) between breakfast eating and health outcomes. These studies didn't account for overall lifestyle differences between breakfast eaters and skippers. Recent controlled trials show that whether you eat breakfast has minimal impact on weight loss or metabolism. Your body is perfectly capable of functioning without breakfast if you're not hungry—you won't enter 'starvation mode' or harm your metabolism.
questions.scientificBasis: Multiple randomized controlled trials have found that breakfast consumption doesn't significantly affect weight loss or metabolic rate compared to skipping breakfast. A comprehensive review published in the BMJ found that breakfast recommendations for weight loss aren't supported by evidence. The key is overall diet quality and listening to hunger signals.
questions.exceptions: Children and teens, people who are pregnant, and people with diabetes on insulin or other glucose-lowering medicines should follow advice from their own clinician on meal timing.

questions.question: Should I stretch before exercising?
questions.answer: No, static stretching before exercise doesn't prevent injury and may reduce performance. Dynamic warm-ups are more effective.
questions.description: Long static stretches (holding a stretch for a minute or more) right before exercise don't reliably prevent injury and can briefly reduce strength and power. A dynamic warm-up that gradually raises your heart rate and rehearses the movements you're about to do is a better use of the time. Short static stretches inside a full warm-up are fine, and longer stretching works well after exercise or as a separate flexibility session.

Research shows it doesn't significantly prevent injuries. A proper warm-up should increase blood flow, raise body temperature, and prepare neuromuscular pathways for the specific movements you'll perform. Dynamic stretching accomplishes this while static stretching doesn't. Post-exercise stretching, when muscles are warm, is ideal for improving flexibility.
questions.scientificBasis: Systematic reviews find that pre-exercise static stretching has little effect on overall injury risk. A 2016 review found the performance drop is mostly seen with stretches held 60 seconds or longer, and is small or absent with shorter stretches included in a full dynamic warm-up.

questions.answer: Avoid it when you can. Glass or ceramic is the safer choice; if you do use plastic, only use containers labeled microwave-safe and replace them when they're scratched or warped.

These chemicals are endocrine disruptors that may affect development, reproduction, and other bodily functions. The effects of long-term, low-level exposure are still being studied, but minimizing exposure is prudent. Fat and acid in foods increase chemical migration from plastic.

The FDA regulates food-contact plastics and no longer allows BPA in baby bottles, sippy cups, or infant formula packaging; scientists continue to study the effects of long-term, low-level exposure.

questions.question: Should I charge my phone overnight?
questions.answer: Yes, it's safe to charge your phone overnight. Modern smartphones have protections against overcharging and battery damage.
questions.description: Modern smartphones use lithium-ion batteries with built-in charging management systems that prevent overcharging. Once the battery reaches 100%, the phone stops drawing significant power from the charger. Many phones now have features like optimized charging that slows charging near 100% or learns your schedule to minimize time at full charge. Overnight charging won't damage your battery any more than daytime charging, though keeping batteries between 20-80% can theoretically extend their lifespan slightly.
questions.reasoning: Lithium-ion batteries can be damaged by staying at 100% charge for extended periods, but modern phones mitigate this with intelligent charging systems. They use trickle charging near full capacity and often stop charging at 100% until the battery drops slightly. The battery management system prevents overcharging damage. The concern about overnight charging comes from older battery technologies that actually could be harmed by overcharging, but this isn't relevant to modern devices.
questions.scientificBasis: Battery research shows that modern charge management systems effectively protect lithium-ion batteries from overcharge damage. Many abstainers in these studies were former heavy drinkers who quit due to health problems, making the abstainer group appear less healthy. When properly controlled studies are conducted, no health benefits emerge from alcohol consumption at any level. Alcohol is metabolized into acetaldehyde, a toxic compound that damages DNA and causes cancer. Even small amounts increase risk of breast cancer, liver disease, and other conditions.

questions.question: Should I avoid cracking my knuckles?
questions.answer: No, cracking your knuckles doesn't cause arthritis or joint damage. It's generally harmless, though some people find it annoying.
questions.description: Despite the common warning, cracking your knuckles has not been shown to cause arthritis or harm your joints. The pop comes from a gas cavity forming in the fluid that lubricates the joint. One doctor who cracked only his left hand's knuckles for about 60 years found no arthritis in either hand, and larger studies agree. Some older research hinted at hand swelling or weaker grip in habitual crackers, but the findings are inconsistent.
questions.reasoning: Pulling or bending a finger joint lowers the pressure inside it, and dissolved gas rapidly forms a bubble in the synovial fluid; real-time MRI in 2015 captured this cavity forming at the moment of the crack. It takes about 20 minutes for the gases to redissolve, which is why you can't crack the same knuckle again right away. This process doesn't damage cartilage or bone. Pain, swelling, or reduced movement in a joint is a different matter and worth getting checked.
questions.scientificBasis: A 2011 study in the Journal of the American Board of Family Medicine found no association between habitual knuckle cracking and hand osteoarthritis. Dr. Donald Unger's six-decade self-experiment, published in 1998, earned an Ig Nobel Prize in 2009. A 2015 MRI study in PLOS ONE showed the sound is linked to cavity formation within the joint.

Muscle cramps while swimming are usually caused by dehydration, overexertion, or poor conditioning—not food in your stomach. The Red Cross and other swimming safety organizations have removed this guidance because there's no evidence supporting it. The real swimming dangers are lack of supervision, exhaustion, and alcohol consumption.

Appetite naturally decreases during illness, which is normal, but this doesn't mean you should avoid eating when hungry.

questions.answer: No, you should not put cotton swabs or any objects inside your ear canal. Your ears are self-cleaning.

The ear canal has tiny hairs and a self-cleaning mechanism that moves wax outward. Cotton swabs push wax back toward the eardrum, where it can accumulate and harden, potentially causing hearing loss, pain, or infection. They can also scratch the ear canal or puncture the eardrum. The satisfying feeling of using cotton swabs actually comes from stimulating nerves, not from necessary cleaning.

questions.question: Should I avoid double-dipping chips in shared dip?

questions.question: Does shaving make hair grow back thicker?
questions.answer: No, shaving doesn't change hair thickness, color, or growth rate. This is a persistent myth with no scientific basis.
questions.description: Shaving cuts hair at the skin's surface but doesn't affect the follicle beneath the skin where hair growth occurs. Hair appears thicker after shaving only because you're seeing the blunt end of the hair shaft rather than the naturally tapered tip. The hair may also feel coarser temporarily because short stubble is more noticeable than longer hair. Shaving has no effect on hair color, thickness, or growth rate—these are determined by genetics and hormones, not by cutting the hair shaft.
questions.reasoning: Hair grows from follicles located beneath the skin surface. When you shave, you're cutting the hair shaft above the skin, which has no biological connection to the living part of the hair in the follicle. The follicle determines hair characteristics like thickness, color, and growth rate. The myth likely persists because freshly shaved hair is more noticeable—the blunt tip feels rough, and short dark hair contrasts more with skin. As hair grows longer, it tapers naturally and becomes less noticeable. Additionally, people often start shaving during puberty when hormones are naturally causing hair to become thicker and darker, creating false correlation.
questions.scientificBasis: Dermatological research has repeatedly demonstrated that shaving doesn't alter hair structure or growth. Clinical studies measuring hair before and after shaving show no changes in thickness, growth rate, or color. The myth has been thoroughly debunked by dermatologists and hair growth researchers.

questions.question: Do I lose most of my body heat through my head?
questions.answer: No, you don't lose more heat through your head than other uncovered parts of your body. This is a myth.

The head may feel more sensitive to cold because it has many nerve endings and because we rarely cover it compared to other body parts. In cold weather, your body prioritizes maintaining core temperature and blood flow to vital organs. Blood vessels in extremities constrict to reduce heat loss, which is why fingers and toes get cold first. Your head, containing your brain, maintains strong blood flow, which can make it feel warmer and may contribute to the myth.
questions.scientificBasis: Thermal physiology research shows that heat loss is proportional to surface area. Studies measuring heat loss from different body parts found no special heat-loss properties of the head. The myth has been debunked by physiologists and thermal regulation experts. While wearing a hat in cold weather is advisable, it's for general warmth, not because of disproportionate heat loss.

questions.answer: Yes. A 5-10 minute dynamic warm-up improves performance and, in sports, structured warm-up programs reduce injuries.
questions.description: A good warm-up starts with light aerobic movement, then adds dynamic moves that rehearse what you're about to do: leg swings, lunges, arm circles, skips, or lighter sets of your main lift. It raises muscle temperature, heart rate, and coordination.
questions.reasoning: Warm muscles contract more forcefully and nerve signals travel faster. Gradually increasing intensity also lets your heart and lungs catch up instead of being hit with sudden demand. Structured programs that combine running, strength, balance, and agility drills have the best evidence for preventing injury.
questions.scientificBasis: A cluster-randomized trial in the BMJ found the FIFA 11+ warm-up program reduced injuries in young female soccer players by about a third, and later reviews support similar reductions across sports.

questions.question: Should I take short breaks from sitting?
questions.answer: Yes. Getting up and moving for a couple of minutes every 30 minutes or so is good for your body, whether you sit or stand at work.
questions.description: Long, uninterrupted sitting is linked to poorer blood sugar control and other health risks. Short breaks don't need to be workouts: walking to get water, taking stairs, or pacing during a phone call all help.
questions.reasoning: Muscle contractions help clear glucose and fats from the blood. Breaking up sitting keeps muscles active through the day in a way that a single workout doesn't fully replace. Breaks also reduce stiffness and give your eyes a rest from screens.
questions.scientificBasis: In a 2012 randomized crossover study in Diabetes Care, interrupting sitting with 2 minutes of light walking every 20 minutes lowered after-meal blood glucose by about a quarter compared with uninterrupted sitting. Guidelines encourage reducing sedentary time alongside regular exercise.

questions.question: Should I keep a consistent sleep schedule?
questions.answer: Yes. Going to bed and waking up at about the same time every day, weekends included, supports better sleep and health.
questions.description: Your body clock regulates sleepiness, hormones, and body temperature on a roughly 24-hour cycle. Irregular sleep times, like staying up late and sleeping in on weekends, shift that clock back and forth, which can feel like jet lag and make it harder to fall asleep on Sunday night.
questions.reasoning: A stable wake-up time is the strongest anchor for your body clock, especially when combined with morning light exposure. Consistency helps you fall asleep faster and wake more easily. If you can't sleep, getting up and doing something calm until you feel sleepy is better than lying awake.
questions.scientificBasis: A 2024 study of about 60,000 UK Biobank participants in the journal Sleep found that sleep regularity predicted mortality risk more strongly than sleep duration did. Sleep medicine guidelines recommend consistent sleep and wake times as a core healthy sleep habit.

questions.question: Should I use screens right before bed?
questions.answer: It's better not to. Try to put phones, tablets, and laptops away 30-60 minutes before bed.
questions.description: Bright screens late in the evening can delay melatonin release and make you feel more alert. Often the bigger problem is the content itself: messages, news, games, and endless feeds keep your brain engaged and push bedtime later.
questions.reasoning: Light, especially blue-rich light, signals daytime to your body clock. Night modes and dimming help somewhat, but the stimulation of interactive content and the 'one more video' effect cost more sleep for many people. Reading a paper book or listening to something calm are better wind-down options.
questions.scientificBasis: In a 2015 controlled study published in PNAS, reading on a light-emitting e-reader before bed suppressed melatonin, delayed the body clock, and took participants about 10 minutes longer to fall asleep compared with reading a printed book. The effect is real but modest, which is why habits around content matter too.

questions.question: Should I quit smoking even if I've smoked for years?
questions.answer: Yes. Quitting at any age improves your health, and the earlier you quit, the more years of life you gain.
questions.description: Benefits begin quickly: within months, circulation and lung function improve, and within a few years the risk of heart attack and stroke drops substantially. Over the following decade, risks of many cancers fall. Most people need several attempts, so a relapse is part of the process, not a failure.
questions.reasoning: Smoking damages blood vessels, lungs, and DNA continuously; stopping removes that ongoing damage and lets the body partly repair itself. Using quit-smoking medicines (such as nicotine replacement, varenicline, or bupropion) together with counseling roughly doubles the chance of success compared with willpower alone.
questions.scientificBasis: A large 2013 study in the New England Journal of Medicine found that people who quit before age 40 avoided about 90% of the excess risk of death from continued smoking, and smokers lose at least a decade of life expectancy. Free help is available in the U.S. at 1-800-QUIT-NOW and smokefree.gov.

questions.question: Should I vape?
questions.answer: No, if you don't smoke. For adults who already smoke, switching completely to e-cigarettes is likely less harmful than continuing to smoke, but quitting nicotine altogether is best.
questions.description: E-cigarette aerosol contains nicotine, which is highly addictive and harms the developing brains of adolescents and young adults, plus other chemicals and metal particles. Vaping is far from harmless, and its long-term effects are still being studied.
questions.reasoning: E-cigarettes don't burn tobacco, so they deliver far fewer of the toxicants found in cigarette smoke. That's why they may help some adult smokers quit, but it doesn't make them safe for nonsmokers. Using both cigarettes and e-cigarettes ('dual use') does not deliver the same benefit as quitting smoking completely.
questions.scientificBasis: The CDC states e-cigarettes are not safe for young people, pregnant people, or adults who don't currently use tobacco. Cochrane reviews have found high-certainty evidence that nicotine e-cigarettes help more people quit smoking than nicotine replacement therapy. The 2019 EVALI lung injury outbreak was linked mainly to vitamin E acetate in illicit THC vaping products.

questions.question: Should I get recommended cancer screenings?
questions.answer: Yes. Screening tests recommended for your age and risk can find some cancers early, when they're much easier to treat, or even prevent them.
questions.description: Key U.S. recommendations include colorectal cancer screening from age 45 to 75, mammograms every two years from 40 to 74, cervical cancer screening from 21 to 65, and annual low-dose CT for lung cancer from 50 to 80 for people with a significant smoking history. Prostate cancer screening for men 55-69 is an individual decision to discuss with a clinician.
questions.reasoning: Colonoscopy can remove precancerous polyps before they turn into cancer, and Pap and HPV testing find cervical changes before they become invasive. Screening isn't free of downsides, such as false positives and overdiagnosis, which is why recommendations target the ages and risk groups where benefits outweigh harms.
questions.scientificBasis: The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force bases its screening recommendations on systematic reviews of benefits and harms; it lowered the colorectal start age to 45 in 2021 and the mammography start age to 40 in 2024.
questions.exceptions: People with a strong family history, genetic risk, or prior abnormal results may need earlier or more frequent screening; ask your clinician.

questions.question: Does drinking alcohol raise my cancer risk?
questions.answer: Yes. Alcohol is a known cause of at least seven types of cancer, and risk rises with the amount you drink.
questions.description: Alcohol increases the risk of cancers of the breast, colon and rectum, esophagus, liver, mouth, throat, and voice box. For some, such as breast cancer, risk begins to rise at around one drink a day. Many people are unaware of this link.
questions.reasoning: The body breaks alcohol down into acetaldehyde, which damages DNA. Alcohol also generates oxidative stress, raises estrogen levels, and helps other carcinogens, such as those in tobacco smoke, get into cells. Drinking and smoking together multiplies the risk of mouth and throat cancers.
questions.scientificBasis: The International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies alcohol as a Group 1 carcinogen. The U.S. Surgeon General's 2025 advisory estimated alcohol contributes to about 100,000 cancer cases and 20,000 cancer deaths in the U.S. each year.

questions.question: Should I get my vitamin D level tested routinely?
questions.answer: No, not if you're healthy and have no symptoms. Testing is useful when a clinician suspects deficiency or you have a condition that affects vitamin D.
questions.description: Routine vitamin D testing became very common, but it hasn't been shown to improve health outcomes in people without symptoms. Labs also differ on what level counts as 'deficient', so results can lead to unnecessary treatment.
questions.reasoning: Testing makes sense for people with conditions such as osteoporosis, malabsorption disorders, kidney or liver disease, or symptoms suggesting deficiency. For healthy people, the decision about whether to supplement can usually be made based on age and circumstances without a blood test.
questions.scientificBasis: The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force found insufficient evidence to recommend screening asymptomatic adults for vitamin D deficiency. The Endocrine Society's 2024 guideline suggests against routine testing in the general population.

questions.question: Should I drink coffee?
questions.answer: For most healthy adults, moderate coffee drinking is fine and may even be associated with health benefits. Limit caffeine if you're pregnant, sensitive to it, or it's hurting your sleep.
questions.description: Up to about 400 mg of caffeine a day, roughly four or five cups of brewed coffee, is not generally associated with harmful effects in healthy adults. Coffee drinkers in large observational studies tend to have lower rates of type 2 diabetes, liver disease, and death from all causes, though these studies can't prove coffee is the cause.
questions.reasoning: Caffeine blocks adenosine, the chemical that builds up and makes you sleepy. Its effects last for hours (its half-life is around five hours on average and varies widely), so afternoon coffee can cut into sleep even if you fall asleep fine. Unfiltered coffee such as French press contains compounds that can raise LDL cholesterol; paper-filtered coffee removes most of them.
questions.scientificBasis: The FDA cites 400 mg a day as an amount not generally associated with negative effects in healthy adults. ACOG advises keeping caffeine under 200 mg a day during pregnancy. A 2017 umbrella review in the BMJ found 3-4 cups a day was associated with lower all-cause mortality.
questions.exceptions: People with anxiety, heart rhythm problems, acid reflux, or poorly controlled high blood pressure may need less caffeine. Children and teens should avoid energy drinks.

questions.question: Should I try intermittent fasting to lose weight?
questions.answer: It can work if it helps you eat less overall, but it hasn't proven better than ordinary calorie reduction. Choose the approach you can stick with.
questions.description: Intermittent fasting includes time-restricted eating (such as eating within an 8-hour window) and alternate-day or 5:2 fasting. Some people find a simple eating window easier than counting calories; others find it leads to overeating later or makes them irritable.
questions.reasoning: Weight loss on any plan comes mainly from eating fewer calories over time. Fasting schedules help some people do that. Early trials suggested metabolic benefits beyond weight loss, but larger, better-controlled studies have generally found results similar to standard calorie restriction.
questions.scientificBasis: In a 2020 randomized trial in JAMA Internal Medicine, 16:8 time-restricted eating did not produce significantly more weight loss than eating three meals a day. A 12-month 2022 trial in the New England Journal of Medicine found time-restricted eating plus calorie restriction was no better than calorie restriction alone.
questions.exceptions: Fasting isn't appropriate during pregnancy or breastfeeding, for children and teens, for people with a history of eating disorders, or for people taking insulin or other glucose-lowering medicines without medical supervision.

questions.question: Should I use ear candles to remove earwax?
questions.answer: No. Ear candling doesn't remove earwax and can cause burns, blockages, and eardrum damage.
questions.description: Ear candling involves placing a hollow, wax-coated cone in the ear and lighting the far end, supposedly creating suction that draws out wax. The residue found inside the candle afterward is candle wax, not earwax.
questions.reasoning: Measurements show no meaningful suction or warmth reaching the ear canal. Reported injuries include burns to the face and ear, candle wax dripping into the ear canal, and perforated eardrums. Since ears clean themselves, most people need no wax removal at all.
questions.scientificBasis: The FDA has warned consumers not to use ear candles, citing reports of burns and other injuries and the lack of evidence of benefit, and has taken action against companies marketing them with health claims.
questions.exceptions: If you have hearing loss, fullness, or pain from earwax, see a clinician. Over-the-counter softening drops are an option for many people without eardrum problems.

questions.question: Should I use medication after its expiration date?
questions.answer: Generally no. Many medicines lose only some potency over time, but some can fail when you need them most, so replace expired medicines, especially critical ones.
questions.description: The expiration date is the last date the manufacturer guarantees full potency and safety when stored properly. A U.S. military program found many stockpiled drugs remained potent well past their dates under ideal storage, but home storage is rarely ideal, and you can't tell potency by looking.
questions.reasoning: Losing potency matters most for medicines where a reliable dose is critical: insulin, nitroglycerin, epinephrine auto-injectors, liquid antibiotics, anticonvulsants, and eye drops (which can also become contaminated). Expired medicines should be disposed of through take-back programs or the FDA's household disposal guidance.
questions.scientificBasis: The FDA advises against using expired medicines because their potency and safety can no longer be assured. Stability studies show results vary widely by drug, formulation, and storage conditions.
questions.exceptions: In an emergency such as anaphylaxis, if the only epinephrine auto-injector available is expired, allergy experts generally advise using it rather than nothing, then calling emergency services.

questions.question: Should I take antibiotics for a cold?
questions.answer: No. Colds are caused by viruses, and antibiotics don't work against viruses.
questions.description: Antibiotics kill bacteria, not the rhinoviruses and other viruses behind colds, most sore throats, and most bronchitis and sinus infections. Taking them won't help you recover faster and can cause side effects such as diarrhea, allergic reactions, and C. difficile infection.
questions.reasoning: Every course of antibiotics also gives resistant bacteria an advantage, contributing to infections that are harder to treat. Rest, fluids, and over-the-counter symptom relief are the treatment for colds, which usually last 7-10 days.
questions.scientificBasis: The CDC estimates that at least 28% of antibiotics prescribed in U.S. outpatient settings are unnecessary, many of them for viral respiratory infections. Antibiotic resistance causes millions of infections in the U.S. each year.
questions.exceptions: See a clinician if symptoms last more than 10 days, you have a high fever, trouble breathing, or symptoms improve and then get worse, as these can signal a bacterial infection.

questions.question: Should I follow the 20-20-20 rule for screen time?
questions.answer: Yes, it's a simple way to ease eye strain: every 20 minutes, look at something about 20 feet away for at least 20 seconds.
questions.description: Long stretches of close screen work cause digital eye strain: tired, dry, or burning eyes, blurry vision, and headaches. Looking into the distance relaxes the focusing muscles, and taking a moment away reminds you to blink.
questions.reasoning: People blink much less often while concentrating on a screen, which dries the eyes. Regular breaks, blinking, artificial tears, positioning the screen slightly below eye level about an arm's length away, and reducing glare all help. Eye strain is uncomfortable but doesn't cause permanent damage.
questions.scientificBasis: The American Academy of Ophthalmology recommends the 20-20-20 rule for computer users. Small studies show short-term symptom relief, though high-quality long-term evidence is limited.
questions.exceptions: If you have persistent blurry vision or headaches, get an eye exam; you may need glasses or an updated prescription.

questions.question: Does sitting close to the TV damage my eyes?
questions.answer: No. Sitting close to a TV or screen doesn't damage your eyes, though it can cause temporary eye strain.
questions.description: This warning dates back to early color TVs, some of which emitted small amounts of X-rays before standards were tightened. Modern screens don't pose that risk. Children can focus up close much more easily than adults, so they often sit close without discomfort.
questions.reasoning: Viewing distance doesn't change the structure of the eye. Long periods of close-up focusing can cause tired eyes, but that fades with rest. Separately, research suggests children who spend more time outdoors are less likely to become nearsighted.
questions.scientificBasis: The American Academy of Ophthalmology states that sitting close to the TV won't damage children's eyes. It does advise that a child who consistently sits very close may be nearsighted and should have an eye exam.

questions.question: Will eating more carrots improve my eyesight?
questions.answer: No, not if you already get enough vitamin A. Carrots help prevent deficiency-related vision problems, but they won't sharpen normal vision.
questions.description: Carrots are rich in beta-carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A, essential for the retina and night vision. In places where vitamin A deficiency is common, it's a leading cause of preventable childhood blindness. In well-nourished people, eating extra carrots won't improve eyesight.
questions.reasoning: The legend got a boost during World War II, when the British publicized carrots as the secret to their pilots' night-time success, reportedly to help conceal their use of radar. A diet rich in vegetables and fruit is good for long-term eye health, but no food corrects nearsightedness or other refractive errors.
questions.scientificBasis: Vitamin A deficiency causing night blindness and xerophthalmia is well documented by the World Health Organization. There's no evidence that consuming vitamin A beyond adequate levels improves vision.

questions.question: Does sugar make kids hyperactive?
questions.answer: No. Controlled studies have found that sugar doesn't affect children's behavior or attention.
questions.description: The belief is extremely widespread, but double-blind studies, where neither parents nor children know who got sugar, show no difference in behavior. Excitement at parties and holidays, where sugary foods are common, is a likely explanation for what parents notice.
questions.reasoning: Expectations strongly shape what adults see. In one experiment, mothers who were told their sons had been given sugar rated them as more hyperactive and watched them more critically, even though the children had received a placebo. There are good reasons to limit added sugar, such as dental health, but behavior isn't one of them.
questions.scientificBasis: A 1995 meta-analysis of 16 double-blind, placebo-controlled studies published in JAMA found that sugar does not affect the behavior or cognitive performance of children, including children with ADHD.

questions.question: Is it dangerous to wake a sleepwalker?
questions.answer: No. Waking a sleepwalker won't harm them, though they may be confused. The best approach is to gently guide them back to bed.
questions.description: The myth that waking a sleepwalker causes a heart attack or shock is false. Sleepwalkers can be disoriented if woken abruptly, and occasionally may react defensively, so speak calmly and avoid grabbing them.
questions.reasoning: Sleepwalking happens during deep non-REM sleep, and the brain is partly awake and partly asleep. The real danger is injury from falls, stairs, or going outside. Locking doors and windows, using stair gates, and removing tripping hazards help keep sleepwalkers safe.
questions.scientificBasis: Sleep medicine experts note there is no evidence that waking a sleepwalker is harmful, while leaving them to wander carries real risk of injury.

questions.question: Should I clean cuts with hydrogen peroxide?
questions.answer: No. Rinse minor cuts with clean running water instead. Hydrogen peroxide and rubbing alcohol can damage healthy tissue and slow healing.
questions.description: The fizzing of hydrogen peroxide looks like it's working, but it harms the new cells your body needs to repair the wound. For a minor cut, stop the bleeding with gentle pressure, rinse with water, wash around the wound with soap, apply petroleum jelly, and cover it with a bandage.
questions.reasoning: Clean water removes dirt and most bacteria without injuring tissue. Keeping the wound moist with petroleum jelly and covered helps it heal faster and reduces scarring compared with letting it dry out and scab.
questions.scientificBasis: First-aid guidance from Mayo Clinic and the American Academy of Dermatology recommends cleaning wounds with water and avoiding hydrogen peroxide and iodine on the wound itself because they can irritate and damage tissue.
questions.exceptions: Get medical care for deep or gaping cuts, bleeding that won't stop after 10 minutes of pressure, animal or human bites, or signs of infection. Check that your tetanus shot is up to date.

questions.question: Should I put butter or ice on a burn?
questions.answer: No. Cool a burn under cool running water for about 20 minutes, then cover it loosely with a clean, non-stick dressing.
questions.description: Butter, oils, and other home remedies trap heat in the skin and can increase infection risk. Ice is too cold and can damage tissue further. Cool (not icy) running water stops the burning process and reduces pain and damage, and it helps even if you start within a few hours of the burn.
questions.reasoning: Skin keeps burning after the heat source is removed. Cooling with water draws heat out and limits how deep the injury goes. Remove rings, watches, and tight clothing near the burn before it swells, but don't pull away anything stuck to the skin. Don't pop blisters.
questions.scientificBasis: Burn first-aid guidelines, including those from Mayo Clinic and burn associations, recommend cool running water and advise against ice, butter, and ointments for fresh burns.
questions.exceptions: Call emergency services or seek urgent care for large burns, deep burns, burns on the face, hands, feet, genitals, or major joints, chemical or electrical burns, and burns in young children or older adults.

questions.question: Should I tilt my head back to stop a nosebleed?
questions.answer: No. Sit up, lean forward, and pinch the soft part of your nose firmly for 10-15 minutes.
questions.description: Tilting your head back sends blood down your throat, where it can make you choke or vomit, and doesn't stop the bleeding. Leaning forward lets blood drain out of your nose, and steady pressure on the soft part (not the bony bridge) lets a clot form.
questions.reasoning: Most nosebleeds come from small blood vessels at the front of the nose. Continuous pressure is what stops them, so resist checking every minute. Afterwards, avoid blowing your nose, bending over, or heavy lifting for a day.
questions.scientificBasis: First-aid guidance from Mayo Clinic and ear, nose, and throat specialists recommends sitting upright, leaning forward, and pinching the nostrils closed for 10-15 minutes.
questions.exceptions: Seek emergency care if bleeding lasts more than 20 minutes, follows a head injury, involves a lot of blood, or causes difficulty breathing. Frequent nosebleeds are worth discussing with a clinician.

questions.question: Should I pee on a jellyfish sting?
questions.answer: No. Urine doesn't help and can make the sting worse. Rinse with vinegar or seawater, remove tentacles, and soak in hot water.

questions.reasoning: Hot water immersion, as hot as you can tolerate without scalding (about 40-45 C / 104-113 F) for 20-45 minutes, helps break down venom and reduce pain. Rubbing the area or applying fresh water can fire more stinging cells. Recommendations vary somewhat by species, so follow local lifeguard advice.
questions.scientificBasis: Medical reviews and first-aid guidance, including from Mayo Clinic, recommend vinegar rinsing for many species and hot-water immersion for pain, and advise against urine, fresh water, and rubbing.
questions.exceptions: Call emergency services for trouble breathing, chest pain, confusion, or a sting covering a large area, and for stings from box jellyfish in areas where they occur.

questions.answer: No. Don't cut, suck, ice, or put a tourniquet on a snakebite. Call emergency services, stay calm, and keep still.

questions.scientificBasis: First-aid guidance from Mayo Clinic and the CDC advises against incision, suction, tourniquets, and ice, and recommends getting to medical care as quickly as possible.

questions.answer: Usually not. The blister's roof protects the skin underneath from infection. Cover it, and only drain it carefully if it's large and painful.
questions.description: A blister is a protective cushion of fluid over damaged skin. Leaving it intact lets new skin form underneath with lower infection risk. Cover it with a loose bandage or moleskin with a hole cut for the blister.
questions.reasoning: If a blister is big, painful, or likely to burst anyway, it can be drained with a sterilized needle at its edge, leaving the overlying skin in place, then covered with petroleum jelly and a bandage. Don't peel off the roof.
questions.scientificBasis: The American Academy of Dermatology recommends leaving blisters intact when possible and gives guidance for safely draining large, painful ones.
questions.exceptions: People with diabetes or poor circulation should see a clinician for foot blisters. Seek care for blisters with signs of infection, such as pus, spreading redness, or warmth.

questions.question: Should I use a car seat for my child on every trip?
questions.answer: Yes. Use a car seat or booster that fits your child's age and size on every ride, and keep children under 13 in the back seat.
questions.description: Car seats are designed for children's bodies, which adult seatbelts don't fit. Keep children rear-facing as long as their seat allows, then forward-facing with a harness, then in a booster until the adult belt fits properly, typically around 4 feet 9 inches tall.
questions.reasoning: In a crash, rear-facing seats spread forces across a child's back and support the head and neck. Boosters position the lap belt across the hips instead of the soft belly. Many seats are installed incorrectly, so free inspections by certified technicians are worth using.
questions.scientificBasis: NHTSA reports that car seats reduce the risk of fatal injury by 71% for infants and 54% for toddlers in passenger cars. Car crashes remain a leading cause of death for children in the U.S.

questions.question: Should I text while driving?
questions.answer: No. Reading or sending a text takes your eyes off the road for about five seconds, enough to cover the length of a football field at highway speed.
questions.description: Distracted driving kills more than 3,000 people a year in the U.S. Texting is especially dangerous because it takes your eyes, hands, and attention off driving all at once. Hands-free calls still split your attention.
questions.reasoning: Driving requires constant scanning and rapid reactions. Even a few seconds of looking away can mean missing a stopped car or a pedestrian. Put your phone on 'Do Not Disturb While Driving', let a passenger handle messages, or pull over somewhere safe.
questions.scientificBasis: NHTSA data show distraction-affected crashes kill thousands of people each year. Most U.S. states ban texting while driving, and many ban handheld phone use entirely.

questions.question: Should I leave a child or pet in a parked car with the windows cracked?
questions.answer: No, not even for a few minutes. A parked car heats up fast even on mild days, and cracked windows barely help.
questions.description: Cars act like greenhouses. Even when it's around 70 F (21 C) outside, the inside of a closed car can climb into the 100s F within an hour, with most of that rise happening in the first 15-30 minutes. Children's bodies heat up three to five times faster than adults', and dogs cool themselves poorly.
questions.reasoning: Dozens of U.S. children die in hot cars each year, most often because they were forgotten. Build habits that prevent this: put your bag or phone in the back seat, and always check the back before locking the car. If you see a child alone in a hot car, call 911.
questions.scientificBasis: A 2005 study in Pediatrics measured an average rise of about 40 F (22 C) inside closed cars within an hour, regardless of the outside temperature, and found that cracking the windows had little effect.

questions.question: Should I shelter under a tree during a thunderstorm?
questions.answer: No. Trees attract lightning, and sheltering under one is one of the most dangerous places to be. Get inside a building or a hard-topped vehicle.
questions.description: There is no safe place outdoors during a thunderstorm. If you can hear thunder, you're close enough to be struck. Lightning can jump from a tree to a person standing nearby, or travel through the ground.
questions.reasoning: Enclosed buildings with plumbing and wiring, and hard-topped metal vehicles, protect you by carrying current around you. A car's protection comes from its metal shell, not its rubber tires. Open shelters like picnic pavilions, tents, and dugouts don't protect you. Wait 30 minutes after the last thunder before going back out.
questions.scientificBasis: The National Weather Service's guidance is 'When thunder roars, go indoors.' It also notes lightning can and does strike the same place more than once; the Empire State Building is hit around 20 times a year.

questions.answer: Yes. Test smoke alarms monthly and replace each alarm 10 years after its manufacture date.
questions.description: Working smoke alarms roughly halve your risk of dying in a home fire. Install them inside every bedroom, outside each sleeping area, and on every level, including the basement. Interconnected alarms, where one sounding triggers them all, give the earliest warning.
questions.reasoning: Most fatal home fires happen at night while people are asleep, and smoke can make you sleep more deeply rather than wake you. Batteries die and sensors degrade, so an alarm that's mounted but not working gives false confidence. Make and practice a home escape plan with two ways out of each room.
questions.scientificBasis: The National Fire Protection Association reports that three of every five U.S. home fire deaths occur in homes with no smoke alarms or no working smoke alarms.

questions.question: Should I have a carbon monoxide detector at home?
questions.answer: Yes. Install carbon monoxide (CO) alarms on every level of your home and near sleeping areas, especially if you have fuel-burning appliances or an attached garage.
questions.description: Carbon monoxide is colorless and odorless, so you can't detect it without an alarm. It comes from furnaces, water heaters, gas stoves, fireplaces, generators, and cars. Early symptoms such as headache, dizziness, nausea, and confusion are easily mistaken for flu.
questions.reasoning: CO binds to hemoglobin much more strongly than oxygen, starving the brain and heart of oxygen. People who are asleep or intoxicated can die before noticing symptoms. Never run a generator, grill, or car in a garage, basement, or near windows, and have fuel-burning appliances inspected yearly.
questions.scientificBasis: The CDC reports that more than 400 people in the U.S. die each year from unintentional CO poisoning not related to fires, and many thousands more need emergency care.
questions.exceptions: If a CO alarm sounds, get everyone outside to fresh air immediately and call 911 or your fire department.

questions.question: Should I let leftovers cool on the counter before refrigerating them?
questions.answer: No. Refrigerate leftovers within two hours of cooking (one hour if it's above 90 F / 32 C). Hot food can go straight into the fridge.
questions.description: Bacteria multiply fastest between 40 F and 140 F (4-60 C), the 'danger zone'. Leaving food out to cool keeps it in that range for hours. To cool large amounts quickly, divide them into small, shallow containers.
questions.reasoning: Modern refrigerators can handle warm food. Some bacteria, like those that cause food poisoning from rice and stews, form toxins that reheating doesn't destroy, so the time food spends in the danger zone matters. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3-4 days or freeze them.
questions.scientificBasis: USDA food safety guidance recommends refrigerating perishable food within two hours, using shallow containers for fast cooling, and reheating leftovers to 165 F (74 C).

questions.question: Should I wash raw chicken before cooking it?
questions.answer: No. Washing raw chicken doesn't make it safer and splashes bacteria around your kitchen. Cooking it to 165 F (74 C) kills the bacteria.
questions.description: Raw poultry often carries Salmonella and Campylobacter. Rinsing it spreads droplets of contaminated water onto sinks, counters, and nearby foods, especially foods that won't be cooked, like salad.
questions.reasoning: Washing can't remove all bacteria anyway, and cooking to a safe internal temperature kills them reliably. Pat chicken dry with paper towels if needed, then throw them away and wash your hands. Use a separate cutting board for raw meat, and check the temperature with a food thermometer.

questions.question: Should I thaw frozen meat on the counter?
questions.answer: No. Thaw meat in the refrigerator, in cold water, or in the microwave. Counter thawing lets the outside warm into the bacterial danger zone.
questions.description: As frozen meat sits at room temperature, its surface warms above 40 F (4 C) long before the center thaws, giving bacteria hours to multiply. The refrigerator is the safest method, though it takes about a day for every 5 pounds of meat.
questions.reasoning: For faster thawing, seal the meat in a leak-proof bag and submerge it in cold tap water, changing the water every 30 minutes, then cook it right away. Food thawed in the microwave should also be cooked immediately. You can also cook meat straight from frozen; it just takes about 50% longer.
questions.scientificBasis: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service guidance lists refrigerator, cold water, and microwave thawing as the only safe methods and warns against thawing on the counter.

questions.question: Is food safe to eat if I pick it up within five seconds?
questions.answer: No. Bacteria can transfer to dropped food in less than a second. More time means more transfer, but there's no safe window.
questions.description: Whether dropped food picks up harmful germs depends mostly on how moist the food is and how contaminated the surface is, not just time. Wet foods like watermelon pick up the most bacteria; dry foods like candy pick up less. Carpet transferred fewer bacteria than tile or stainless steel in testing.

But the risk is real where surfaces may be contaminated, such as kitchen floors after raw meat prep, and for young children, older adults, and people with weakened immune systems.

questions.question: Should I use a password manager?
questions.answer: Yes. A password manager lets you use a long, unique password for every account without having to remember them.
questions.description: Reusing passwords is one of the biggest risks online: when one site is breached, attackers try the same email and password on banks, email, and shopping sites ('credential stuffing'). A password manager generates and stores strong passwords and fills them in for you.
questions.reasoning: Password managers also help protect against phishing, because they won't fill in your password on a look-alike site with the wrong address. Protect the manager itself with a strong, unique master password and multi-factor authentication. Built-in options from your browser or phone are much better than reusing passwords.
questions.scientificBasis: NIST's Digital Identity Guidelines require services to allow password managers and paste, and CISA recommends password managers as a core step for staying safe online.

questions.question: Should I turn on two-factor authentication?
questions.answer: Yes. Turn on multi-factor authentication (MFA) for your important accounts, starting with email, banking, and your password manager.
questions.description: MFA requires a second proof that it's you, such as a code from an app, a security key, a passkey, or a text message, in addition to your password. Even if your password is stolen or guessed, an attacker usually can't get in without that second factor.
questions.reasoning: Not all methods are equally strong. Passkeys and hardware security keys resist phishing best, authenticator apps are next, and text-message codes are weakest but still far better than nothing. Save your backup codes somewhere safe so you don't get locked out.
questions.scientificBasis: Microsoft has reported that MFA blocks more than 99.9% of automated account-compromise attacks. CISA urges everyone to enable MFA and recommends phishing-resistant methods where available.

questions.question: Should I use a VPN all the time?
questions.answer: Not necessarily. Most of your web traffic is already encrypted with HTTPS. A VPN is useful in specific situations but isn't a cure-all for online safety.
questions.description: A VPN encrypts traffic between your device and the VPN provider, hiding it from the local network and your internet provider. That can help on untrusted public WiFi or when you need to appear to be in another location. It doesn't stop phishing, malware, tracking cookies, or logging into sites as yourself.
questions.reasoning: Using a VPN shifts trust from your network or internet provider to the VPN company, which can see your traffic metadata. Free VPNs in particular may collect and sell data. Keeping devices updated, using HTTPS, a password manager, and MFA matter more for most people.
questions.scientificBasis: The FTC notes that most websites now encrypt the information you send, and that VPNs can add protection on public networks but vary widely in trustworthiness.

questions.question: Should I install software updates promptly?
questions.answer: Yes. Install updates for your operating system, browser, and apps soon after they're released, and turn on automatic updates.
questions.description: Many updates fix security vulnerabilities that attackers already know about and actively exploit. Once a fix is published, attackers can study it to target people who haven't updated. Delaying updates leaves known doors open.
questions.reasoning: Most successful attacks use known, already-patched weaknesses rather than new ones. Automatic updates remove the need to remember. Devices that no longer receive security updates, such as old phones and routers, should be replaced when possible.

questions.question: Should I let my phone battery drain to 0% before charging?
questions.answer: No. Lithium-ion batteries don't need full discharges. Charge whenever it's convenient; frequent partial charges are actually gentler.
questions.description: The advice to fully drain batteries comes from older nickel-cadmium batteries, which had a 'memory effect'. Modern lithium-ion batteries have no memory effect, and deep discharges add extra wear.
questions.reasoning: Lithium-ion batteries age faster when kept at very high or very low charge, and especially when hot. Staying roughly between 20% and 80% minimizes wear, but the difference for most people is modest. Phones include battery management to protect against harmful extremes.
questions.scientificBasis: Battery research summarized by Battery University shows partial discharge cycles cause less wear than full cycles for lithium-ion cells. Phone makers recommend avoiding high temperatures and using built-in optimized charging features.

questions.answer: Yes. Fast charging with your phone's own or a certified charger is safe. It may add slightly more battery wear, mainly from extra heat.

questions.answer: No. Rice doesn't dry phones well and can leave dust and starch inside. Unplug everything, tap out the water, and let the phone air-dry.
questions.description: Rice absorbs moisture slowly and only from its surroundings, not from inside the phone's sealed spaces. Small particles can get into ports. Air flow does more than rice.

Don't use a hair dryer, heat, or compressed air, and don't push cotton swabs into ports. Many modern phones are water-resistant, but not waterproof, and resistance decreases with age.

questions.question: Should I try to reduce how much plastic I use?
questions.answer: Yes. Using less plastic, especially single-use items, does more for the environment than recycling.
questions.description: Most plastic ever made has ended up in landfills or the environment rather than being recycled. Practical swaps include reusable bags, bottles, and containers, buying in bulk, choosing products with less packaging, and skipping disposable cutlery and straws you don't need.
questions.reasoning: Plastic is made mostly from fossil fuels, and its production creates greenhouse gas emissions. Plastic in the environment breaks down into microplastics that are now found in water, soil, food, and human tissue; their health effects are still being studied. Reducing use cuts waste at the source.

questions.answer: No. A modern, full dishwasher typically uses much less water and energy than washing the same dishes by hand.

questions.answer: No. Modern fuel-injected cars need only about 30 seconds before driving. Driving gently warms the engine faster than idling.
questions.description: Long warm-up idling was necessary for older carbureted engines. Today's engines are designed to be driven soon after starting. Idling wastes fuel, adds emissions, and doesn't warm the transmission, tires, or other parts that only warm up when the car moves.
